problem: Outdoor zero-shot object navigation must rely on RGB only because targets lie beyond depth range, so distant targets shrink to a few pixels and visibility flickers between faint, partial and fully occluded. Prior outdoor ZSON methods (end-to-end policies, LLM reasoning, ray-based semantic projection) and tiny-object detectors do not handle this coupled failure, giving unstable headings and delayed decisions.
motivation: Applications like search and rescue, field inspection and post-disaster assessment need robots to head toward targets 100+ m away. Depth-based semantic maps do not work at that range, and modest viewpoint changes or foreground structures easily occlude few-pixel targets, so a consistent heading cannot come from direct observation alone. The paper observes that localized semantic contrast within aligned tile groups gives a stable regional saliency usable for both direction and visibility.
key_idea: Build an aligned multi-scale CLIP tile pyramid with variance-weighted bottom-up saliency fusion to get a stable coarse regional saliency, and reuse that saliency for visibility detection, keyframe heading memory, direction fusion and active search.
insight: The perception ablation shows the multi-scale pyramid is the most critical part for far range: at 150 m error rises from 51.0 to 130.0 without it, to 100.5 without saliency amplification, and to 70.5 without hierarchical fusion. The navigation ablation shows visibility detection matters most (SR 40.3 to 12.7, RSR 82.6 to 52.4). Active search buys recovery success at the cost of longer recovery path (RPL 18.4 without vs 22.7 with). A high RSR does not translate into high SR, since detection failures, time limits and overshoot dominate.
method: Tile pyramid: a single-resolution RGB image is partitioned into dyadically aligned tile levels (8x12, 4x6, 2x3); CLIP scores each tile against the text prompt, and each coarse tile deterministically covers 4x4 fine tiles.

Hierarchical target-saliency fusion: parent scores are updated bottom-up as s' = s + beta*sum of Top-k child scores (Top-2 for T1->T2, Top-1 for T2->T3), with beta = base^sigma_hat (base 1.5) from child-set std, amplifying groups with high local contrast.
Target direction: the center pixel of the coarse-level max tile is back-projected with intrinsics K and extrinsics/odometry into a world-frame direction vector.
Visibility detection: per-level sparsity ratio r_l = max/(mean+eps) and std are thresholded (thresholds adopted from ApexNav); the target is visible if any level passes.

Keyframe memory and direction fusion: when visible, keyframes (salient tile features, world direction, 6-DoF pose) are stored in a sliding window; under occlusion, historical headings are fused by saliency-weighted, time-decayed averaging to guide frontier selection.

Active search and fallback: on invisibility, go to the frontier along the last heading, scan ±30°, and accept a tile only if it matches the prompt and keyframe features; after repeated failures, return to the last keyframe and do a 360° look-around.
Integration: plugged into an occupancy-grid frontier exploration framework using depth + odometry for obstacle avoidance and frontier detection.

setting.backbone: CLIP (frozen) for tile scoring plus hand-designed saliency fusion and frontier exploration
setting.observation: egocentric RGB (stereo camera) + depth + odometry; LiDAR (MID360) used for mapping in real world
setting.action_space: frontier selection on an occupancy grid with local planning and obstacle avoidance (continuous ground robot motion)
setting.simulator: TartanAir dataset (perception); a custom 200 m x 170 m outdoor simulation (navigation); real-world campus
setting.privileged: none (initial observation of the target is needed to bootstrap; GT directions used only for evaluation)

numbers_note: Baseline comparison for long-range perception is given only in a figure (not extractable). Real-world experiment is qualitative with no numeric results. Abstract claims 82.6% heading maintenance and 17.5% SR improvement.
results: On the custom outdoor simulation, the method reaches RSR 90.5/73.3/84.0 and SR 42.0/38.5/40.5 for short/long/mixed occlusion, versus the strongest baseline RayFront (RSR 75.5/41.7/59.7, SR 27.0/22.5/23.0), though its recovery path length is longer. For perception on TartanAir it keeps penalized angular error at 51.0 at 150 m where ablated variants reach 70.5-130.0, and a real campus run (350x450 m) succeeds qualitatively.
limitations: Struggles with long-term occlusion, and needs an initial observation of the target to bootstrap; SR stays around 40% despite high RSR.
Recovery path length is higher than baselines because of look-around and active search, and the planner lacks reasoning ability in cluttered scenes.
Evaluation is on a custom simulation and a single qualitative real-world run, with no quantitative real-world results.
